newsitem.title: USA: Up to 245,000 people in N.Y.C. might lose benefits.
newsitem.headline: Up to 245,000 people in N.Y.C. might lose benefits.

text.p: The New York City Council on Wednesday said that next year as many as 245,000 of its citizens and legal immigrants could lose benefits like Food Stamps and Medicaid under the new federal welfare reform bill.
Federal aid for New York City for such programs could be slashed by as much as $370 million.

Legal immigrants, whose benefits are curtailed under the new federal program, would suffer the brunt of the cutbacks, with as many as 130,000 of them losing Food Stamps. And more than 66,000 citizens also would lose these noncash benefits.

But the council's forecasts might prove a worst case scenario, as the Clinton Administration has said that it would seek to temper some of the new welfare bill's impact on these programs, a staff member of the city council explained.
The full effects of the new federal welfare bill on New York State and the city are not yet known because the welfare task force set up by Gov. George Pataki has not finalized its recommendations.
The group on Thursday holds the last meeting needed to let it draft a basic program it then can send to Washington by early next week for its approval.

At least 25 states already have submitted their plans to Washington and New York's slower approach had been criticized as starting on October 1, it qualified for an extra $20 million for every month by which it beat the July 1 deadline.

The lack of a state plan and confusion about the federal law's intent makes it hard for the city to forecast the new bill's impact, a deputy directory for the city Office of Management and Budget said at a Council hearing.

But one issue appeared clear: the city, which accounts for about 66 percent of the state's welfare caseload, was afraid that it would not get a fair share of the state's $2.4 billion block grant. "We are extremely, extremely interested in getting the city's fair share of welfare dollars," said Lisa Parrish. The deputy director estimated the city will spend $1.4 billion for welfare programs.

The Council fretted the state might use any extra monies to help close its future budget gaps instead of paying for welfare. Any windfalls that could result if the economy strengthens, allowing more people to find jobs, could be big.

Should welfare caseloads fall three percent a year, the new program that replaces Aid for Families with Dependent Children could give the state a stream of bigger surpluses, rising from $458 million in 1997 to $727 million in 2002.

But if the economy turns down, the risks could be substantial, as city council staffers noted that welfare caseloads rose for five years after the 1990 recession, which was considered a mild one for the nation as a whole.

The council's forecasts are much rosier than ones by the Congressional Budget Office. It said that if welfare caseloads were to rise three percent a year, the windfall would shrink from $353 million in 1997 to $19 million in 2002.

Nor are these the only potential, major expenses facing the city. The costs of creating jobs for welfare recipients to meet the new federal requirements and provide them with childcare could prove substantial, city council staffers said.

They estimated that in 1997 the city would have to have about 58,000 people who collect welfare under the program that replaces Aid for Familes with Dependent Children in work-related activities. While a total of more than 64,000 people are expected to be involved in such activities in 1996, the new federal laws would slash this number by not counting education and setting a one-fifth allowence for job training.

Further, restricting federal benefits in one area could cause people whose benefits were curtailed to apply for other types of benefits, like the state-funded Home Relief program for adults, they said.
The range of programs whose caseloads could rise is fairly broad. For example, children from impoverished families are more likely to be placed in foster care.
